svg.desc: Banner for a paper showing that a universal-inference split likelihood-ratio interval, recomputed after every new pair of observations, is not a confidence sequence. A chart plots one exact simulated path of the log split likelihood ratio at the true parameter, Q_n = (S_n T_n − T_n²/2)/n, against the number of observation pairs n on a logarithmic axis from 1 to 100 million. A dashed orange horizontal line marks the fixed threshold log 5 used at the 80% level; red dots mark the five separate times the blue path rises above it, near n = 25 to 40 and again near one million, so the recomputed interval excludes the true value again and again. A green curve, the repaired threshold of Theorem 5 with a normal-mixture boundary, rises slowly with n and the path stays under it throughout. A side panel says how slow the damage is: the error first exceeds the stated level when the last look is about 100 times later than the first at 80%, about 10 to the 4 times at 95% and about 10 to the 9 times at 99% (Gaussian continuum limit, the last extrapolated), and that the long-run guarantee is zero in any model. The path uses a fixed seed; seeds 1 and 2 do not cross before 100 million and paths vary widely.
svg.text: Keep checking a split likelihood-ratio interval, and it will exclude the truth

fixed threshold log 5 (80% level): crossed again and again
Qn = log split likelihood ratio at the truth (one exact simulated path)
